metadata.title: The Slopling's Odyssey
metadata.author: AI Assistant
metadata.description: A tragicomic odyssey about an AI-assisted coder, a self-described 'slopling', who is offered a team-lead role. The ladder says up is the only way. He loves the work itself. Call, Voyage, Return: through Scylla and Charybdis, the Inbox Sea, Bell Works, the Cyclops of calibration, and the Underworld where Ajax won't speak, to an orchard where a father might finally see his son instead of his title.

suggestedTheme.reason: Literary and dark with warm brass accents. It carries both the mock-epic solemnity and the bruised warmth of a tragicomedy about craft and fathers.

beats.name: The Slopling
beats.notes: ASSET: Open-plan office at dusk, one monitor glowing with a chat window full of code. INTENT: Establish that his mastery is invisible. The meters introduced here (Craft, Standing, Cunning, Meaning, Leverage) are the story's state.

parameters.text:
Your name is Odie Marsh. You are twenty-nine, and your craft is one the culture is still arguing about. On LinkedIn you wrote *AI-assisted software engineer*. In the group chat you are a **slopling**, a slopfeeder, an AI code proompter. You spend your days coaxing a language model into writing billing code. You steer it away from cliffs it cannot see, and you catch the confident lies it tells at 4 p.m. on a Friday.

Nobody can see the part you're good at. The diff looks the same whether you felt the bug coming or the model got lucky.

On a Tuesday, Dana from Engineering books a fifteen-minute meeting titled *Quick chat :)*. The smiley face is how you know.

beats.name: Dana's Offer
beats.notes: INTENT: The Call to Troy. Dana is a warm studio-comedy boss type (type-echo only). The leverage gained here makes the renegotiate option succeed later.

dialogTree.speaker: Dana
dialogTree.text: Odie! Sit, sit. So. I'm going to say two words and I want you to hear them the way I mean them. Team. Lead. Five reports, the Agentic Velocity squad, a real title. You'd be prompting the people who prompt the machines. Which, honestly, when I say it out loud, is a little bit of a joke at its own expense. But it's a *good* joke! It's a joke with equity.

choices.text: Why me?

dialogNode.speaker: Dana
dialogNode.text: Because your velocity chart looks like a ski jump. Because the VP asked who ships, and I said you, and then everyone looked at me like I'd have to prove it. The ladder needs a face on it, Odie. Yours tested well.

choices.text: So it's the chart you're promoting, not the work.

dialogNode.speaker: Dana
dialogNode.text: It's the chart I can *show* people. The work... I believe you about the work. I just can't put it in a slide. That's not a me problem, that's a slides problem.

choices.text: [Continue]
That's... really kind. Thank you.

dialogNode.speaker: Dana
dialogNode.text: Don't thank me, thank the ski jump. Think it over. Friday?

choices.text: [Continue]
What happens to my code?

dialogNode.speaker: Dana
dialogNode.text: You'd... oversee code. Code-adjacent. You'd be in the code *spiritually*. One-on-ones, roadmap, a little light headcount strategy. The machines write it, the team prompts it, you prompt the team. It's prompts all the way down!

choices.text: Then who keeps the theory of the billing service alive? It lives in my head, not the repo.

dialogNode.speaker: Dana
dialogNode.text: ...That's the scariest question anyone has asked me this quarter, and I sat through the board's AI strategy offsite. Write that down. No, don't write it down, they'll make it a KPI.

choices.text: [Continue]
Right. Prompts all the way down.

dialogNode.speaker: Dana
dialogNode.text: That's the spirit! Friday!

choices.text: [Continue]
Can I think about it?

dialogNode.speaker: Dana
dialogNode.text: Of course! Take until Friday. Take the whole Friday. Take... until ten a.m. Friday.

choices.text: [Continue]

beats.name: The Greeks on the Beach
beats.notes: INTENT: Colleagues as the assembled Greeks at Aulis. Introduces the future Suitors (Chad, the Brad-type smooth talker; Dougie, the fail-upward type) and Ines, the apprentice.

parameters.text:
By lunch, it has leaked. Someone posts a party-parrot emoji in #general, and then forty more. Chad Bellweather starts a slow clap that the whole floor joins. He once presented your refactor at all-hands so fluently that the VP thought it was his. Dougie Pratt has been 'about to ship' the same feature since spring. He hugs you and says, 'Bro. *Bro.*' Only Ines Duarte, the junior who sends you questions at eleven at night, doesn't clap. She watches from her desk as if she's counting something.

It feels like the beach at Aulis: the assembled Greeks, cheering, pushing a man toward a ship he hasn't said he'll board. Nobody asks if you want to go to Troy. Troy is *up*. Up is where you go.

Then your phone rings. Dad.

beats.name: Father on the Phone
beats.notes: INTENT: The father is seen through the son's guesses, as Telemachus guesses at Odysseus. His meters (Father's Sight, Father's Pride) appear here. Recognition is what the story is after; pride is what the ladder feeds.

dialogTree.speaker: Lars
dialogTree.text: Your mother saw it on the LinkedIn. Team lead.

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *A pause long enough to hear the kettle in his kitchen. You try to read it the way you read him your whole childhood: from the pauses and the half-sentences, from what his hands did while his mouth didn't.*

dialogNode.speaker: Lars
dialogNode.text: Well. Well, well. My boy, in charge.

choices.text: Dad, it's a desk job. I'd stop building things.

dialogNode.speaker: Lars
dialogNode.text: Building things is how you earn the desk.

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *He says it like a rule he learned somewhere, a rule that cost him something. You've never been sure what.*

choices.text: When did you stop building things, Dad?

effects.reflectionText: My son asked when I stopped building things. Nobody has asked me that in thirty years.

dialogNode.speaker: Lars
dialogNode.text: ...Your mother's calling me. Congratulations, son. I mean it.

choices.text: Yeah. I know, Dad.

dialogNode.speaker: Lars
dialogNode.text: Good lad. Ring us Friday.

choices.text: Thanks, Dad. I knew you'd be proud.

effects.reflectionText: My son is going to lead people. Dad drove a forklift for forty years. Now look.

dialogNode.speaker: Lars
dialogNode.text: Proudest I've been since the graduation. Your grandad drove a forklift forty years. Now look at you.

beats.name: Knowing How
beats.notes: INTENT: Ryle and Naur framing. The contested question: is the theory in his head or in the model's weights?

parameters.text:
That night, in the flat, you can't sleep. You keep turning over a distinction from a philosophy elective: Gilbert Ryle's *knowing that* versus *knowing how*. You can know *that* a bicycle stays upright for reasons of physics. Knowing *how* to ride it lives in the legs.

Then there's Peder Naur, stern and Danish. In *Programming as Theory Building* he argued that a program's real substance isn't the code at all. It's the living theory in the programmer's head: why the program is shaped this way, and what it would mean to change it. When nobody practises that theory anymore, the program decays even if every file survives.

So here is the question you can't put down. What happens to the theory in your head if you stop practising it? And a worse one underneath: is the theory even in *your* head? Or is it in the model's weights, and you're just the guy holding its hand?

beats.name: The Desk at 1 a.m.
beats.notes: INVESTIGATION LOOP: each description returns to beat_10, which can loop back here. effectsOncePerChoice prevents farming Leverage.

parameters.question: Your desk, at 1 a.m. Three things on it seem to be looking at you.

props.name: Prompt Journal
props.description: A battered notebook where you log every time the model was wrong and you knew before the tests did.

props.name: Brass Calipers
props.description: Your father's old vernier calipers, given to you at twelve with no explanation.

props.name: Offer Letter
props.description: The PDF Dana sent, printed, because printing makes things real.

parameters.text:
You flip through the journal.

*Mar 3: model invented a VAT rule for Norway. Smelled wrong before I knew why. Rounding was too clean.*
*Apr 19: it 'fixed' the retry loop by deleting the retry.*
*Jun 2: three hours steering it away from a beautiful refactor that would have broken invoicing for every customer in Québec.*

There are two hundred entries, and none of them are visible in the repo. The repo shows only the code that survived. This notebook is the closest thing you have to Naur's theory written down, and Naur would say even this is just its shadow. Still, whoever replaced you would not have it. Slowly, you realise that this is leverage.

beats.name: The Calipers
beats.notes: INTENT: Plants the father's buried craft. This is the key to Laertes's orchard ending.

parameters.text:
The calipers are cold and precise; the jaws still close without a hair of light between them. Dad gave them to you at twelve and said only, 'Look after those.'

You know almost nothing about why. You know he was a toolmaker at the Hendry works before you were born. You know he became a foreman at thirty-four and never stood at a lathe again. You know there's an orchard behind your parents' house where he grafts apple trees with a patience he never once showed at the dinner table.

You've always guessed, the way Telemachus guessed at a father he barely knew, that the title meant something to him you were never old enough to be told. You put the calipers in your bag.

beats.name: The Offer Letter
beats.notes: INTENT: Graeber's taskmaster fear, turned back on his own prompting work.

parameters.text:
*Team Lead, Agentic Velocity.* The raise would pay off your student loan in two years. Under Responsibilities, the first bullet reads *Grow headcount*. The second reads *Drive alignment*. No bullet mentions writing, reading or understanding any code at all.

You think of David Graeber's *Bullshit Jobs* and the category he called 'taskmasters': people whose job is to supervise people who don't need supervising, or to invent work for others. He wrote that knowing your job is a performance does a kind of 'spiritual violence.' Then, uncomfortably, you think of your own days spent typing wishes into a box. Is *that* a performance too?

One more line in the PDF: the role must be filled by the end of the quarter. They need you more than the smiley face let on.

parameters.question: It's late. The flat hums. What now?

choices.text: Look at the desk again
Answer Ines's 11 p.m. message about the billing retry
Go to bed. Friday will come either way.

parameters.text:
You don't send her the fix. You send her the theory. Why the retry exists, and which customer it saved in 2023. What the model will try to 'simplify' if she lets it. How it *feels* when the model is about to be confidently wrong: the answer that's too clean, the suspicious politeness.

It takes forty minutes. She replies: 'oh. OH. ok that's actually the whole job isn't it.'

You feel oddly happy. Nobody will ever see those forty minutes on a dashboard.
Friday. The meeting is at ten. Dana has booked the room called Olympus. Of course she has.

beats.name: Scylla and Charybdis: The Call
beats.notes: MAJOR CHOICE. Accept and Decline are Scylla and Charybdis. Renegotiate succeeds only if Leverage >= 3 (checked at beat_15). Stall hands the decision to a Slack poll (randomTarget).

parameters.speaker: Dana
parameters.question:
Olympus, ten a.m. Dana, two HR people and a bowl of sad clementines. 'So!' says Dana. 'Ithaca or Troy? Kidding. Team lead or...?'

Ahead of you, as in every story about men in boats, wait two monsters. On one side is Scylla, six-headed: the promotion that eats a little more of you every sprint. On the other is Charybdis: the whirlpool of declining, which swallows careers whole and leaves behind a reputation for 'lacking ambition.' No ship sails between them without losing something.

choices.text: Accept. Take the chair, like the brilliant makers who took it before you.
Decline. Stay at the workbench and let them call it a lack of ambition.
Renegotiate: 'What if I lead the craft instead of the people?'
Stall. Feign madness. Plough the sprint board with salt.

parameters.text:
You say yes. The HR people exhale. Dana does a small fist-pump she will deny later. You think of every brilliant maker in every studio comedy who finally gets the big chair and spends season two learning that the chair has opinions.

As you leave, Chad grips your shoulder. 'Huge, man. Huge. Let me know if you need help with the people stuff.' He says *people stuff* the way a fox says *henhouse*.

Dana, beaming, approves six weeks of sabbatical before the reorg. 'Go learn how leaders lead. Read things. Meet weird geniuses. Come back a captain.'

You say no. The silence in Olympus has a specific texture, like a quiz-show buzzer that forgot to buzz. One HR person writes something down. Dana says 'Totally valid!' in the voice of someone updating a spreadsheet.

In the corridor you feel like Ajax walking back to his workbench. Or like the server-room nihilist in every startup farce, who treats status as a bug report about other people. Either way, you're free. Either way, you're alone.

Dana recovers and approves six weeks of sabbatical anyway. 'Cool off. Think. The role will be... somewhere. When you get back.' Chad is already walking toward her office.

You lay it out. No reports. A craft role instead: you own the theory of billing, review the model's output across teams, and train whoever wants to learn the work. You mention, calmly, that the billing service has exactly one living theory, that it's in your head, and that the quarter ends in nine weeks. You mention the journal.

Dana looks at HR. HR looks at the clementines. 'Fine,' says Dana. 'Senior Craft Lead. It's a new box on the chart. I'll have to explain the box.'

People usually only pull this move with a Nobel in their pocket. You pulled it with a notebook. Before you start, six weeks of sabbatical: 'Figure out what the box is for.'

You lay it out: a craft role, no reports. Dana's smile goes very still. 'Odie, I love that. I *love* that. But the chart only has rungs. There isn't a box for really good at the thing. If there were, everyone would want to be in it.'

HR writes something down. By the time you're back at your desk, the word going round is *difficult*. Dana approves six weeks of sabbatical in the tone of someone opening a window to air out a room.

beats.name: Odysseus at the Plough
beats.notes: COMEDY: Palamedes put Telemachus in front of the plough. Here Dana drags the production database into the furrow.

parameters.text:
You do what Odysseus did when the recruiters came to Ithaca: you pretend to have lost your mind. You arrive at Olympus wearing a headset with no cable and announce that you are ploughing the sprint board. You drag tickets into a column you have named SALT. You yoke the Jira bot to the coffee machine. You speak only in commit messages: 'wip.' 'fix.' 'fix fix.' 'final final (2).'

It's going brilliantly until Dana, who has read the same myth, calmly drags the production database into your furrow. Your hand shoots out to protect it before you can stop yourself. Sanity: revealed.

'Okay,' says Dana. 'Since you're clearly not deciding, the team will.' A Slack poll goes out. Your career is now a Slack poll.

The poll closes. Eleven votes for you, two for Dougie (one of them Dougie's). Congratulations: you are a team lead, appointed by acclamation while pretending to be a ploughman. Your father is told it was unanimous.

Dana grants six weeks of sabbatical, 'to, you know. Recover.'

The poll closes. Dougie Pratt wins, mostly because he voted for himself four times from different devices and nobody checks. While you were busy salting a Jira board, he was named interim team lead. His victory speech includes the phrase 'synergy horizon.'

Dana grants you six weeks of sabbatical, 'to, you know. Recover.'

beats.name: Act Break: Snapshot (act1_end)
beats.notes: Bookmark act1_end is referenced at beat_98: has the father's recognition grown during the Voyage and Return?

beats.name: Departure
beats.notes: ASSET: A ferry café dissolving into a ship's deck. INTENT: The Voyage is a half-dreamed sabbatical through tech history.

parameters.text:
The sabbatical begins on a Monday, which feels like a cruelty. You meant to read three leadership books on a beach. Instead you fall into the long, half-dreamed odyssey every engineer falls into eventually: podcasts at double speed, old conference talks, forum archaeology, biographies read in a ferry café until the café becomes a ship and the ship becomes a myth.

On the first night out, a figure sits down across from you, laptop open, sticker reading *vibes*. It's Andrei Karpathi, the man who gave your whole craft its name, and therefore, you suspect, its punchline.

beats.name: Karpathi: Blessing and Teardown
beats.notes: INTENT: The contested craft. Is his metis real but new, or is the model holding the theory? Karpathi coined 'vibe coding'; no direct quotes are attributed to him beyond the term.

dialogTree.speaker: Andrei Karpathi
dialogTree.text: I named it vibe coding, you know. As a half-joke. The idea was you give in to the vibes and forget the code even exists. You just ask, and accept, and keep going. People took it... very seriously. Is that what you do?

choices.text: No. I don't forget. I read every diff. I argue with it.

dialogNode.speaker: Andrei Karpathi
dialogNode.text: Then you're not vibing. You're steering. Which is interesting! But here's the uncomfortable bit: is steering a skill, or a habit the next model release makes obsolete?

choices.text: It's metis. Practical judgement under uncertainty. Knowing when the model is confidently wrong.

dialogNode.speaker: Andrei Karpathi
dialogNode.text: James C. Scott's word. Good. The sailor's feel for weather that no manual captures. Maybe that's what you have. Ryle would say you can't fully write it down. Naur would ask whose head the theory lives in, yours or the weights'. I genuinely don't know. Neither do you. That's what makes it a real question.

choices.text: [Continue]
Honestly? Maybe the model holds the theory and I just hold the leash.

dialogNode.speaker: Andrei Karpathi
dialogNode.text: Then the test is simple, if brutal. Change the tool and see what's left in you. If something's left, it was yours.

choices.text: [Continue]
Argue with me properly. Out loud. As long as it takes.
Everyone says the real skill now is reading rooms, not diffs.

dialogNode.speaker: Andrei Karpathi
dialogNode.text: Polymetis. Odysseus's kind of intelligence: many turns, many tricks, the talker who wins the armour. It's real. Promotions love it. But it's a different animal from the craftsman's know-how. Ask Ajax how that contest went.

choices.text: [Continue]

beats.name: Open Argument with Karpathi
beats.notes: AI RUNTIME: Optional free-form debate about whether AI-mediated work counts as real know-how. The fallback exit keeps the story moving.

parameters.scenario: A ferry café at night that keeps turning into a ship's deck. Odie, an AI-assisted coder offered a team-lead role, debates with Andrei Karpathi whether steering a coding model is genuine know-how (Ryle's knowing-how, Scott's metis, Naur's theory building) or whether the model holds the real theory.
parameters.npcPersonality: Playful, curious, generous, and unwilling to flatter. Takes both sides seriously, keeps asking where the theory actually lives, and enjoys the irony that he named the craft he is now taking apart.
parameters.openingLine: Okay, let's really do it. I'm Andrei, the person who named your job as a joke. You think steering the model is a craft. Convince me. What do you know that the model doesn't?

action.steerPrompt: Bring in Peder Naur's idea that a program's real substance is the theory in the programmer's head, and ask whether that theory fades if the tool changes.

directions.npcExitMessage: Wish him well on the voyage and say the question will follow him to every island.

parameters.fallbackExitMessage: Say the ship is leaving, that the question is still open, and that he should go and see how others answered it.
parameters.systemInstructions: Keep replies under 80 words. Never invent direct quotations attributed to any real person. Discuss ideas, not quotes. Stay warm and tragicomic. Satirise the career ladder, never the people.

beats.name: Circe's Offsite
beats.notes: MONSTER: Circe is the transformation from craftsperson into taskmaster. Moly is the protected coding hour.

parameters.question:
Before you've even left harbour, your new-manager onboarding arrives: a mandatory offsite on the island of Aiaia, which is an Airbnb in a former bottling plant. The facilitator introduces herself only as Circe. She has a lanyard, a soothing voice and a framework. 'We'll begin,' she says, handing round little cups, 'by unlearning the urge to *do the work yourself*.'

Across the room, three new leads from Sales and Platform are already gently turning into swine. They say 'let's take this offline' to each other in a way that sounds like grunting.

choices.text: Drink the framework.
Eat the moly: block one sacred coding hour a day and tell Circe it's non-negotiable.

parameters.text:
Then the winds of the backlog take the ship. You had a plan, an orderly itinerary of thought leaders, but the sea has other ideas, and you wake up beached on an island you didn't choose.

That is how odysseys work. It is also how sabbaticals work.

beats.name: The Chart of Islands (Hub)
beats.notes: HUB: Islands already visited are hidden by variables. The Charter Room appears only with Leverage >= 5. After 4 islands, beat_63 sends the player to the Underworld.

parameters.question: The chart lies across the café table, which is a ship's deck, which is a café table again. Islands visited: ${islandsVisited} of 4 before the long way home. Each island is ruled by someone who lived a different answer to your question. Where do the winds take you next?

choices.text: Brookes's Ledger, an island made of paper
The Inbox Sea, where something is singing
Bell Works Garden, where the fruit tastes like afternoon
The Oracle, a cave lit by GPU fans
The Flat Island, which has no managers
Carmick's Exile Workshop, a shed on a cold coast
Hassaby's Charter Room, golden, and open to you
Knuthe's Cave, reached by a ladder that goes down
The Road of Older Ladders, running inland to the sea
The Calibration Cave, home of a single glowing eye

parameters.text:
Brookes's Ledger is an island made of paper. Fred Brookes is there, white-haired and courteous, at a desk the size of a mainframe. He said yes. Long ago he was asked to manage one of the biggest software projects on earth, and he took the chair. Then he did what almost nobody on the ladder does: he wrote down what it cost.

The ledger lies open. One column holds what management bought: scale, influence, a famous book. The other holds what it charged. At the bottom, in his own neat hand, is the law that bears his name, the one your whole industry quotes and nobody obeys: adding people to a late software project makes it later.

dialogTree.speaker: Fred Brookes
dialogTree.text: 'People think the law is about schedules,' he says. 'It's really about theory. The understanding in people's heads doesn't pour into new hires like water. Every new person needs it explained, and explaining is work, and the explainers stop building.' He turns the ledger toward you. 'Ask what you came to ask.'

choices.text: Was it worth it? Saying yes?

dialogNode.speaker: Fred Brookes
dialogNode.text: 'I learned things I could only learn in the chair. And I wrote them down so you wouldn't have to sit in it to know them.' He taps the cost column. 'That's the trade. If you say yes, keep a ledger. Most people don't. That's how the ladder stays mysterious.'

choices.text: [Continue]
Can I copy the law? For the next headcount meeting.

dialogNode.speaker: Fred Brookes
dialogNode.text: 'Of course. Though I warn you: managers love to quote it right before they hire anyway.' He smiles. 'A law nobody obeys is still a law. It just turns into a joke you tell at your own expense.'

choices.text: [Continue]
Read the cost column without asking anything.

dialogNode.speaker: Fred Brookes
dialogNode.text: *He lets you read in silence. Time not spent designing. Friends who stopped being peers. A decade rich in knowing that and poor in knowing how.* 'Some of that was worth it,' he says at last. 'Some of it was just the price of the chair.'

choices.text: [Continue]

parameters.text:
The Inbox Sea is calm and glassy and full of voices. You already know them. Your new team-lead inbox holds 312 unread messages, and every one of them is singing your name. *Quick sync? Can you weigh in? Looping you in.*

On a rock in the middle sits a mild-mannered man in a cardigan with a laptop, singing too. You have no wax for your ears. You have only a calendar.

The Inbox Sea is calm and glassy and full of voices. You have no lead's inbox of your own to drown in, but you can hear what the sea would have sung to you: *Quick sync? Can you weigh in? Looping you in.*

On a rock in the middle sits a mild-mannered man in a cardigan with a laptop, singing too.

beats.name: Linos Torwald, the Siren
beats.notes: MONSTER: the Sirens are the Inbox. Verified line used word for word in its original context, describing his work as a maintainer.

dialogTree.speaker: Linos Torwald
dialogTree.text: 'I read email, I write email, I do no coding at all any more,' sings Linos Torwald, not unhappily. He built one of the most important pieces of software in the world. He never chose to become a manager. The project just grew around him until the only way to keep shaping it was to read and answer everyone else's work. 'It wasn't a promotion,' he says. 'Nobody offered. The mail just... rose.'

choices.text: Stuff my ears: notifications off. Sail on.

dialogNode.speaker: Linos Torwald
dialogNode.text: 'Sensible. Most people who hear this song think it's about status. It isn't. It's about the code getting too big for one pair of hands. If that happens to your thing, you'll hear the song again.'

choices.text: [Continue]
Lash me to the mast. I want to listen. What did you learn about people?

dialogNode.speaker: Linos Torwald
dialogNode.text: *He tells you about 2018, when he stepped away for a while, very publicly, and said he had to learn to read people better, that he'd been bad at it for a long time.* 'Turns out understanding people is its own craft,' he says. 'Nobody hands you the theory for that either. You build it. Badly, at first.'

choices.text: [Continue]
Confess: I already have 312 unread and I've been in the role for a day.

dialogNode.speaker: Linos Torwald
dialogNode.text: 'Ah. Then you're not sailing past the Sirens. You live here now.' He offers you a folding chair on the rock. 'You can still steer from here. Some of us do. But be honest with yourself about which song you're singing.'

choices.text: [Continue]

beats.name: Bell Works Garden
beats.notes: MONSTER: the Lotus-eaters. Staying costs an extra island slot.

parameters.text:
Bell Works Garden is a brick laboratory gone soft with ivy, and everything in it is play. Claude Shanning rides past on a unicycle, juggling three balls, while a small mechanical mouse solves a maze on the lawn. It learns the maze, remembers it, and runs it perfectly the second time. Ken Tomson is hunched over a terminal, writing something small and perfect that will outlive everyone here.

Nobody has a title. Nobody has a one-on-one. The fruit on the trees tastes like an afternoon that never ends.

dialogTree.speaker: Ken Tomson
dialogTree.text: 'Management here?' Ken Tomson glances up, amused. 'It was just an umbrella, not really a focus of power. Somebody keeps the rain off. The rest of us get on with it.'

dialogNode.speaker: Claude Shanning
dialogNode.text: 'Have a ball!' says Claude Shanning, and throws you one. You catch it. He throws another. 'The mouse,' he adds, wobbling past, 'is called Theseus. He knows the maze because he's walked it. You can't download walking it.'

choices.text: Stay one more afternoon. Then one more.

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *One afternoon becomes nine. It is the happiest you've been in years. You don't write anything down, and you nearly forget there is a father, an office, a question. When you finally stumble back to the ship, the sabbatical calendar has moved on without you.*

choices.text: [Continue]
Who holds the umbrella? Do they ever want to put it down?

dialogNode.speaker: Ken Tomson
dialogNode.text: 'The good ones don't want to hold it at all. That's why it works.' He goes back to his terminal. 'The trouble is, a ladder can't see the umbrella. It only sees who's standing under it looking important.'

choices.text: [Continue]
Thank them and leave while I still can.

dialogNode.speaker: Claude Shanning
dialogNode.text: 'Smart. The lotus here is just fun. Fun is the most dangerous thing there is.' He catches all three balls without looking.

choices.text: [Continue]

parameters.text:
The Oracle sits in a cave lit by GPU fans. Ilya Sutskov, the shaman-leader, presides over a small circle of researchers with his arms raised. 'Feel the AGI!' he chants. They chant it back, the cave hums, and for a moment you do feel something: something vast and indifferent, and coming.

He never wanted to manage anything but the question. He became a CEO anyway. The prophecy business, it turns out, needs a chief executive.

dialogTree.speaker: Ilya Sutskov
dialogTree.text: 'Ask,' says Ilya Sutskov softly. 'The cave will answer. Not always in sentences.'

choices.text: Will what I know survive the next model?

dialogNode.speaker: Ilya Sutskov
dialogNode.text: *The fans spin up. One line appears on every screen: WHICH PART OF YOU IS THE PART THAT KNOWS?* He nods as if this were obvious. 'If the knowing is in the tool, it changes when the tool changes. If it is in you, in how you notice, it moves with you. Only practice tells you which.'

choices.text: [Continue]
Chant along. Feel it.

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *The circle opens to let you in. Someone hands you a hoodie. It feels wonderful to belong to a chant. Only later do you notice that you've stopped asking questions.*

choices.text: [Continue]
How does a prophet end up running payroll?

dialogNode.speaker: Ilya Sutskov
dialogNode.text: *He laughs, surprised.* 'Someone must keep the cave open. If I don't, someone who feels nothing will.' *For a second he looks tired, like any engineer who has just been handed a calendar.* 'That is the bargain.'

choices.text: [Continue]

beats.name: The Flat Island
beats.notes: Verified handbook line, quoted word for word.

parameters.text:
The Flat Island has no managers. At Vane, everyone wheels their desk wherever they like. There are no titles, no org chart, no ladder at all. It's paradise, until you notice that every conversation, every desk-wheel and every decision curves gently toward one man in the centre. Gabe Newall is very relaxed, very kind, and very obviously the sun.

The employee handbook is pinned up beside the coffee machine. One line is highlighted: 'Of all the people at this company who aren't your boss, Gabe is the MOST not your boss.'

dialogTree.speaker: Gabe Newall
dialogTree.text: 'No bosses here,' says Gabe Newall pleasantly, munching something. 'Just people deciding what's worth doing.' Three people nearby immediately decide that what he just said is worth doing.

choices.text: I'll propose it back home: the team doesn't need a lead at all.

dialogNode.speaker: Gabe Newall
dialogNode.text: 'Could work. Could also mean the power's still there and nobody's allowed to say where.' He shrugs, friendly. 'Flat isn't the same as free. You'd have to be honest about the bowing.'

choices.text: [Continue]
Say nothing. Watch whom everyone glances at before they speak.

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *You count. Everyone bows to someone. There is no king, and there is still a kingdom. The ladder isn't gone here; it's been folded so you can't see the rungs.*

choices.text: [Continue]
Wheel my desk into a corner and just build something.

dialogNode.speaker: Gabe Newall
dialogNode.text: 'Good choice. Nobody'll stop you.' He beams. 'Nobody'll notice either, unless it's great. That's the deal.'

choices.text: [Continue]

beats.name: Carmick's Exile Workshop
beats.notes: Verified Carmick lines, quoted word for word in their original context (his departure letter and description).

parameters.text:
Jon Carmick's Exile Workshop is a shed on a cold coast, full of half-built hardware and one enormous whiteboard. He left the vast court of Metta, where the money flowed like the Aegean, for a small, hands-on outfit called Sharp Labs.

His farewell letter is taped to the wall: 'This is the end of my decade in VR.' Below it, underlined: 'We have a ridiculous amount of people and resources, but we constantly self-sabotage and squander effort.' Elsewhere he said he had 'wearied of the fight.'

The shed is very quiet. The coffee is excellent. There's only one mug.

dialogTree.speaker: Jon Carmick
dialogTree.text: 'You want to know if it's worth it,' says Jon Carmick, not looking up from a scope trace. 'Everyone who comes here wants to know that. The work's better. The days are mine. Nobody schedules me into a meeting about the meeting.' A pause. 'It's also just me and the problem. Most nights.'

choices.text: Let me stay a while as your apprentice.

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *He shows you how he thinks: fast, flat, ruthless with his own ideas. For a week you are better than you have ever been. On the seventh night you catch yourself talking aloud to the oscilloscope, because there's no one else.*

choices.text: [Continue]
What does exile cost?

dialogNode.speaker: Jon Carmick
dialogNode.text: 'Influence. You stop steering the big ship. You find out how much of what you called leadership was just being in the room where the money got spent.' He finally looks up. 'And you find out who calls when you're not useful to them.'

choices.text: [Continue]
I couldn't do this. I need people.

dialogNode.speaker: Jon Carmick
dialogNode.text: 'Then don't exile yourself. Build a smaller ship with people on it.' It is, you realise, a third kind of answer.

choices.text: [Continue]

beats.name: Hassaby's Charter Room
beats.notes: MONSTER: Calypso, the golden cage of a redesigned role. Opens only with Leverage >= 5. The costs are shown honestly.

parameters.text:
The Charter Room opens only for those with leverage, and it opens for you. It's a golden room with a nymph's patience in its walls. This is Denis Hassaby's room. At DeepMound he rewrote his own role, from chief executive to chairman and chief scientist, as calmly as editing a config file. It's his pattern: games-studio CEO, then PhD student, then CEO again, then the chair. Each time he stepped back toward the work, the world let him, because by then he had leverage of the Nobel kind.

The costs are framed on the wall too: senior people who left, an investor wobble, a share-price fall on the day the news broke. Someone always pays when a man steps off the ladder. Calypso's island is lovely. Odysseus wept on its beach every day for seven years.

dialogTree.speaker: Denis Hassaby
dialogTree.text: 'Everyone wants this room,' says Denis Hassaby warmly. 'A role shaped exactly to you. The trouble is that it's easy to write a perfect charter and then never leave the room where you wrote it.' He slides a blank page across. 'Write yours.'

choices.text: Draft and redraft the perfect role. Stay until it's flawless.

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *You write it forty times. Each draft is more beautiful. Each day the door is a little further away. When you finally leave, weeks have gone by. The charter is perfect, and you've written no code at all.*

choices.text: [Continue]
Take a rough draft and leave while the door is open.

dialogNode.speaker: Denis Hassaby
dialogNode.text: 'Good. A charter is a tool, not a home.' He walks you out. 'Remember who pays for it. Somebody always picks up what you put down.'

choices.text: [Continue]
Who paid when you stepped back?

dialogNode.speaker: Denis Hassaby
dialogNode.text: 'People I respected left. Investors flinched. Some colleagues had to carry things I'd stopped carrying.' He doesn't look away from it. 'Leverage means you can refuse. It doesn't mean refusing is free.'

choices.text: [Continue]

parameters.text:
You reach Don Knuthe's Cave by a ladder that goes *down*. At the bottom, by lamplight, a gentle old man is working through a problem by hand, perfectly content, with no inbox at all.

He explains, cheerfully, that his job was never to be 'on top of things.' His job is to be 'on the bottom of things': to go down where things actually work, and stay there long enough to understand them all the way through.

dialogTree.speaker: Don Knuthe
dialogTree.text: 'Most people climb to see more,' says Don Knuthe. 'I go down to see better. It's slower. Nobody gives you a title for it.' He chuckles. 'They give you a cave.'

choices.text: Let me sit at the bottom of things with you for a day.

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *You trace a single bug through every layer of the stack, by hand, without the model. It takes nine hours. By the end you understand billing more deeply than two years of prompting ever taught you. You also realise you couldn't have done it without everything the prompting taught you about where to look.*

choices.text: [Continue]
Did you ever keep a ledger, like Fred Brookes?

dialogNode.speaker: Don Knuthe
dialogNode.text: 'Fred went up and wrote down the view. I went down and wrote down the rocks.' He smiles. 'Both are useful. Only one gets you invited to the offsite.'

choices.text: [Continue]
How do I write down what I know for whoever comes after me?

dialogNode.speaker: Don Knuthe
dialogNode.text: 'Explain it to someone,' he says. 'A real person, not a document. Peder Naur had it right: the theory lives in people. So the only way to save it is to grow it in another person.'

choices.text: [Continue]

parameters.text:
The Road of Older Ladders runs inland, crowded with people who rose by going *deeper*. Young Compagnons du Devoir pass you on their Tour de France. They are carpenters and stonemasons walking town to town and workshop to workshop, becoming masters by crossing a country rather than climbing an org chart. In Japan, a potter named a Living National Treasure is honoured not for managing potters but for being the potter, and for teaching.

At Ise, the great shrine is rebuilt every twenty years, a practice said to preserve the past by refreshing the people: the knowledge survives because each generation must actually build it. Scholars recite their ijazah, the chain of teachers who handed a text from person to person back through the centuries. Jean Lave and Etienne Wenger walk among them, taking notes on communities of practice, where newcomers start at the edge and move toward the centre by doing the work.

beats.name: Where the Road Meets the Water
beats.notes: TONE: No comedy here. Mau Piailug is portrayed with respect; no words are put in his mouth.

parameters.text:
At the end of the road, by the sea, the tone of everything changes.

Here the story is of Mau Piailug, master navigator of Satawal, who carried the old art of wayfinding: reading swells, stars, birds and the colour of the water, without instruments. That knowledge was his and his community's to keep. In the 1970s, when few people still held it, he chose to share it with Hawaiians who wanted to sail as their ancestors had. In 1976 he guided the canoe Hōkūleʻa from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti by the old ways. He chose whom to teach, and how, and what.

The ladder he climbed had no rungs anyone could see from an office. It went across the ocean and down through generations.

You don't make any jokes here. You stand where the road meets the water for a long time.

beats.name: What You Carry from the Road

parameters.question: What do you carry away from the Road?

choices.text: Take Ines on properly. Choose to share, as a master chooses.
Resolve to go deeper, not higher, whatever the chart says.
Write to your father about the Compagnons, the Treasures and the canoe.

effects.reflectionText: A letter from my son about carpenters walking France to become masters. He's telling me something about himself. Maybe about me.

beats.name: The Calibration Cave
beats.notes: MONSTER: the Cyclops is the ladder's single eye (Scott's 'seeing like a state'). Being 'Nobody' turns invisible craft into a weapon.

parameters.text:
The Calibration Cave belongs to the Cyclops: an enormous performance dashboard with a single glowing eye. It sees only what can be counted: titles, headcount, tickets closed, lines changed. James C. Scott called this kind of vision *seeing like a state*, making the world legible by flattening it until only the measurable is left.

Every engineer whose mastery left no trace has been eaten here, quietly, during calibration season. The eye swivels to you. 'WHAT IS YOUR NAME,' it booms, 'AND WHAT IS YOUR IMPACT?'

dialogTree.speaker: Narrator
dialogTree.text: The eye waits. Its pupil is a bar chart.

choices.text: 'My name is Nobody.'

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *The dashboard searches. Nobody has no title, no reports, no headcount. Nobody's impact is unattributed. 'NOBODY IS HURTING ME,' it bellows to the other dashboards, which conclude that nothing is wrong and go back to sleep. You walk out clinging to the belly of a sheep-shaped KPI. Invisibility, it turns out, is also cover. And then a funnier thought: if Nobody did the work, maybe Nobody needs the role.*

choices.text: [Continue]
Recite my title, my velocity chart and my headcount plan.

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *The eye glows with satisfaction and lets you pass. As you go, you notice it has kept something: a little of you, the part that wasn't on the chart.*

choices.text: [Continue]
Put out its eye: argue that the metrics measure the wrong thing.

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *You make a brilliant, furious case. The eye blinks, reboots, and is replaced by a slightly larger eye. Still, three engineers who were hiding in the cave follow you out. That's something.*

choices.text: [Continue]

beats.name: Calling Home
beats.notes: INTENT: Penelope's loom from the other side. The calipers unlock the strongest recognition line.

dialogTree.speaker: Lars
dialogTree.text: Hello? Is that you? Your mother's at choir. How's the... sabbatical.

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *He says 'sabbatical' like a word from a foreign language he doesn't approve of. You picture him in the hallway in his socks, holding the phone a little away from his ear. You've been gone long enough to miss him in a way you couldn't explain to him.*

choices.text: Dad, it's like your lathe. You feel the burr before you see it. That's what I do with the model.

effects.reflectionText: He said it's like feeling the burr on the lathe. He remembered. I didn't think anyone remembered I did that.

dialogNode.speaker: Lars
dialogNode.text: *A very long silence.* '...The Hendry lathes. You'd run your thumb along the edge. Nobody taught you that, you just... knew.' *Another silence.* 'I didn't know you remembered I did that.'

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *You didn't, exactly. You guessed. It seems you guessed right.*

choices.text: Share my screen. Show him a session: the model goes wrong, and I catch it.

dialogNode.speaker: Lars
dialogNode.text: 'So it typed all that, and you... you just knew that bit was rubbish?' *A pause.* 'Huh. Go on then. Show me another.'

choices.text: [Continue]
Tell him what sounds impressive: the leaders I've met, the plans, the title.

dialogNode.speaker: Lars
dialogNode.text: 'Good. Good lad. That's how it goes, isn't it. Up.' *He sounds pleased, and somewhere else at the same time.*

choices.text: [Continue]

beats.name: Meanwhile: The Suitors
beats.notes: MONSTER: the Suitors move in while he is away. AI tailors the report to callChoice and stalled; the fallback is complete on its own.

parameters.prompt: Write a short satirical report from the office while Odie is away on sabbatical. Rivals ('the Suitors') are moving in: Chad Bellweather, a smooth room-reader, is quietly taking over his meetings and credit; Dougie Pratt, who fails upward, is claiming his dashboards; Ines Duarte, the junior he mentors, is quietly keeping the billing service alive. If callChoice is 'accept', they're circling his new title. If it's 'decline' or 'renegotiated', they're circling the empty team-lead role. If stalled is true, mention Dougie's interim title. Tragicomic, warm, aimed at the ladder, not the people. No quotes from real people.
parameters.fallbackText: Meanwhile, back at the office, the Suitors are feasting. Chad Bellweather has started 'just covering' your one-on-ones. Dougie Pratt has put his name on your billing dashboard. Someone has booked Olympus every Thursday under the title 'Leadership Vision (Odie TBC).' Only Ines keeps quietly fixing the retry loop the way you showed her, and nobody notices.

parameters.text:
The sabbatical's last week comes, and with it the descent every odyssey owes: the Underworld. It looks a lot like a conference hotel after the conference. Grey carpet, a hum of shades wearing lanyards, the dead of old reorganisations murmuring about roadmaps.

You pour out the offering, a lukewarm oat flat white, and the shades crowd round. One stands apart: huge, silent, still holding a workman's tools. Ajax.

beats.name: Ajax Will Not Speak
beats.notes: Verified lines: 'Let a man nobly live or nobly die' (Ajax, in life) and Odysseus's 'We are dim shapes, no more, and weightless shadows' (pitying Ajax). Both quoted word for word.

dialogTree.speaker: Ajax
dialogTree.text: *He says nothing.* He was the steadiest craftsman at Troy, the one who held the line. When the dead Achilles' armour was awarded, it went not to him but to the better talker, Odysseus, and Ajax went mad with the shame of it. Carved on the rim of his great shield are the words he spoke while he was alive: 'Let a man nobly live or nobly die.' He will not look at you.

choices.text: I'm sorry. You were the better craftsman. They gave the armour to the better talker.

dialogNode.speaker: Ajax
dialogNode.text: *Silence. He turns his face away, exactly as he did in the old story.*

choices.text: We are dim shapes, no more, and weightless shadows.

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *Long ago Odysseus spoke those words about Ajax, refusing to gloat over the man he had beaten. You say them now about both of you, and about everyone on every ladder. Ajax does not answer. But he doesn't walk away either.*

choices.text: [Continue]
Leave him in peace.

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *You step back. The silence follows you like a dog.*

choices.text: [Continue]
I think I might be like you. Steady. And outtalked.

dialogNode.speaker: Ajax
dialogNode.text: *Nothing. Only the tools in his hands shift, the way a craftsman's hands shift when someone talks about the work instead of doing it.*

choices.text: [Continue]
Craft without a voice is how you end up down here.

dialogNode.speaker: Ajax
dialogNode.text: *He doesn't answer that either. Perhaps that is the answer.*

choices.text: [Continue]

parameters.question: Beyond Ajax, the pit shows visions of roads not taken, flickering like old monitors. Which do you look into?

choices.text: Odysseus staying home
Ajax accepting the loss, and living
Mau keeping the knowledge, and Hōkūleʻa never sailing
Climb out of the pit.

parameters.text:
In the first vision, Odysseus's plough-madness works. Nobody calls his bluff. He stays on Ithaca, tending vines, raising his son, never famous. No Troy, no wooden horse, no twenty years at sea.

The vision is lovely and small and, you notice, has no story in it at all, which is exactly what the ladder always says about staying. You wonder whether 'no story' is a loss, or just a story the ladder tells.

In the second vision, Ajax loses the armour and goes home. He is furious for a season. Then he goes back to the forge, takes apprentices, and makes shields that never appear in any epic but stop a thousand spears. He grows old. Nobody sings about him.

He seems, and you can hardly bear to watch it, fine. Better than fine. The armour was a title. The shields were the work.

beats.name: Vision: The Knowledge Kept
beats.notes: TONE: Respectful. Keeping the knowledge was entirely his right; the vision passes no judgement.

parameters.text:
The third vision is quiet, and you watch it with care. In it, Mau Piailug decides the knowledge stays where it is, as was entirely his right. Hōkūleʻa never makes its voyage by the old ways. A generation of Hawaiian navigators never learns the swells and the stars from him.

Nothing in the vision is a judgement; the art was his to give or to keep. What it shows is how much one person's choice to share can carry, and how a craft lives or fades depending on whether someone chooses to pass it on, and to whom.

beats.name: Act Break: Snapshot (voyage_end)
beats.notes: Bookmark voyage_end is referenced at beat_90: did the Return lift or weigh on Odie's mood?

parameters.text:
You come home the way Odysseus did: unannounced, slightly unrecognisable, carrying a sabbatical's worth of thoughts that won't fit in a status update.

The office has been occupied. The Suitors are feasting. Chad Bellweather is running your old standup, saying 'love that' to things he doesn't love. Dougie Pratt has your monitor. A banner from someone's farewell still says CONGRATS ON THE NEXT CHAPTER, and nobody remembers whose.

And at 4 p.m., as if summoned by myth, the billing service goes down.

beats.name: The Bow of Ithaca
beats.notes: INTENT: Stringing the bow makes invisible craft visible for a moment. Gated on Craft, or on having passed the craft on.

parameters.question: It's the great bow of Ithaca: an old, unforgiving service nobody else can string. Chad prompts the model to 'just fix it holistically,' and the model writes a beautiful patch that deletes Québec. Dougie tries rebooting it with confidence. Slowly, everyone turns to look at the stranger at the door.

choices.text: String the bow: walk to the keyboard and fix it, steering the model line by line.
Hand the bow to Ines: 'You know this one. Go.'
Let the Suitors keep trying. It's not your bow anymore.

parameters.speaker: Dana
parameters.question: Afterwards, Dana finds you in the kitchen. 'So, captain. You're back. The chair's still yours, if you want it. Do you?'

choices.text: Keep the chair, with one sacred coding hour a day, defended like Penelope's loom.
Keep the chair fully. The people are the craft now.
Hand it back. Go home to the work.

parameters.text:
Here's the joke the ladder never saw coming: when the reorg finally lands, nobody takes the team-lead role. Not because nobody wanted it, but because the team spent six weeks without one and discovered they mostly needed someone to hold an umbrella. Now they take turns.

Dana writes a long, slightly baffled memo about 'emergent self-direction.' The box on the chart sits empty. It was never load-bearing.

When the reorg lands, the role goes to Ines Duarte. Not because she out-talked anyone, but because over these weeks she became the one people went to. She knew *why* the retry loop existed. She could feel when the model was about to be confidently wrong. And she explained it to the next junior at eleven at night, the way someone once explained it to her.

It's strange to see your own theory alive in another person's head. Peder Naur would call it the only way a program survives. It feels like being a little bit immortal and a little bit replaced. You promise yourself she'll keep her hands on the work. You'll make sure she gets the hour.

When the reorg lands, the role goes to Dougie Pratt, who has never finished a feature but has never once been in the room when one failed. He has failed upward with the grace of a hot-air balloon. His first act is renaming the team 'Velocity Pantheon.' His second is scheduling a meeting to discuss his first act.

It's farce. It's also, you realise, the price of letting other people decide for you.

When the reorg lands, the role goes to Chad Bellweather: smooth, quick, a reader of rooms, the Odysseus of the open-plan office. He gives a speech about craft that quotes your journal without knowing it's yours. The VP loves it. It stings in exactly the place Ajax was stung.

And yet, watching him calm a furious client with a grace you'll never have, you have to admit his polymetis is a real skill too. It just isn't yours, and the ladder can only see one kind.

So you stay in the chair. Some days it's the Inbox Sea; some days it's Circe's island; some days you manage to defend an hour of real work, and it feels like stringing the bow.

Dana tells the VP you're 'growing into it.' You suspect you're also growing out of something.

On the train to your parents' house, you notice you feel lighter than when you climbed out of the Underworld. Not resolved. Lighter. Whatever else the voyage did, it gave you back the sense that the question was yours to answer.

On the train to your parents' house, you notice you feel heavier than when you climbed out of the Underworld. The office kept moving without you, the way offices do. You keep wondering who pays when someone steps off the ladder, or onto it. Maybe the answer is always: someone you didn't think to ask.

beats.name: Ithaca
beats.notes: ASSET: Small semi-detached house, an orchard too big for the garden, an older man grafting in an old jacket. Golden late light.

parameters.text:
Ithaca is a semi-detached house on the edge of a small town, with an orchard behind it too big for the garden. Your father is out there, as you knew he would be, in an old jacket, grafting. He doesn't hear you come up the path.

For a moment you just watch his hands. You realise you've spent your whole life reading him the way you read the model: from what he does rather than what he says. You've never known whether he could read you back.

beats.name: In the Orchard
beats.notes: INTENT: The search for a token like Laertes's trees. The Prompt Journal (inventory) and knowledge of the lathe (calipers) unlock the deepest lines. Recognition shifts here, before the ending checks.

dialogTree.speaker: Lars
dialogTree.text: Oh. It's you. *He doesn't stop grafting.* Your mother said you'd be back. So. Is it team lead now, or what is it? I never know what to tell people.

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *You guess at what's under the question. Forty years of 'what do you do' at weddings. A foreman's badge in a drawer. A man who was told that up was the only direction worth going, and went, and maybe never asked himself whether he wanted to.*

choices.text: Dad, let me show you what my hands do, even though you can't see them. (Hold out the journal.)

dialogNode.speaker: Lars
dialogNode.text: *He wipes his hands, takes it and reads. 'Model invented a VAT rule. Smelled wrong before I knew why.' He reads it again.* 'Smelled wrong,' he says. 'Aye. You get that.'

choices.text: You got it too. At the Hendry works. Why did you stop?

effects.reflectionText: I told my son I missed the lathe. I've never told anyone that.

dialogNode.speaker: Lars
dialogNode.text: 'They offered foreman. Your grandad cried when I told him. Nobody in our family had ever been anything but hands.' *He sets down the grafting knife.* 'I was good on the lathe. Better than good. I never told anyone I missed it, because what kind of man misses being lower down?'

choices.text: Just let him keep reading.

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *He turns pages for a long time. You can't tell what he's thinking; you never could. But he doesn't give it back.*

choices.text: Tell me about the lathe. The one you gave up.

effects.reflectionText: My son asked about the lathe. He knew. Somehow he always knew.

dialogNode.speaker: Lars
dialogNode.text: '...Who told you about that?' *He looks at you for a long time.* 'They offered foreman at thirty-four. Your grandad cried. Nobody in our family had been anything but hands. I was good on the lathe. I never said I missed it. What kind of man misses being lower down?'

choices.text: The same kind as me. (Show him the journal.)

dialogNode.speaker: Lars
dialogNode.text: *He reads. 'Smelled wrong before I knew why.'* 'That's the burr,' he says quietly. 'You feel the burr.'

choices.text: Show him the calipers you still carry.

dialogNode.speaker: Lars
dialogNode.text: *He takes them, closes the jaws and holds them up to the light. No light comes through.* 'Still true,' he says. 'You looked after them.'

choices.text: Just stand with him a while.

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text: *You stand together among the trees. Neither of you says anything for a while, and it isn't the bad kind of silence.*

choices.text: The title's fine, Dad. Tell people whatever sounds good.

dialogNode.speaker: Lars
dialogNode.text: 'Right. Right you are.' *He goes back to his graft. The conversation closes like a gate.*

choices.text: [Continue]

beats.name: Ending Check: Has He Come to See You?
beats.notes: Delta from story start, not a literal threshold. The father starts at 0 recognition; his pride is a separate sentiment.

beats.name: Ending Check: Is the Craft Alive?
Ending Check: Did the Voyage Move Him?
Ending Check: Does the Work Remember?
Naming the Trees
beats.notes: IDEAL ENDING: Odysseus proved who he was to Laertes by naming the trees his father had given him. Here the token is a shared practice: feeling the work before you see it.

dialogTree.speaker: Lars
dialogTree.text: *He's quiet for a long while. Then he points with the grafting knife, the way he used to when you were small.* Go on then. You used to know them all. Name them.

choices.text: Name the trees.

effects.reflectionText: He named every tree, then showed me where his hands were in the code. I'm proud of my son, and now I know what for.

dialogNode.speaker: Narrator
dialogNode.text:
*You name them, the way Odysseus named his father's trees to prove who he was. The Bramley you fell out of at nine. The three Discoveries he planted the year you were born. The grafted tree with four kinds of apple on one trunk, which he calls 'the committee.' The pear that never fruits, which he won't cut down.*

Then, because the trees are a practice you share, you name the other things: the VAT bug, the Québec refactor, the retry loop. You show him where your hands were in a page of code that looks like anyone's.

dialogNode.speaker: Lars
dialogNode.text: 'Four kinds on one trunk,' he says. 'You remembered the committee.' *His voice goes strange.* 'You do what I did. Not the lathe. The feeling for it. The knowing before you know.' *He puts a hand on your shoulder, not on your title.* 'I'm proud of you, son. I always was. I just didn't know what for, until now.'

choices.text: [Continue]

parameters.message:
**Laertes's Orchard**

Your father's pride didn't go anywhere. It moved, off the title and onto you. The token wasn't a badge or a headcount. It was a shared practice: a feel for the work that leaves no mark on the finished thing.

Back at the office, the team-lead role is held by ${roleHolderName}. Your craft is still contested. Nobody knows yet whether it's metis or a borrowed theory the next model will make obsolete. But someone has seen it.

*Questions to carry home:* Can saying no be its own kind of ambition? What would a ladder look like that rewarded going deeper instead of going up? What would it take for every parent to see a child's invisible work as work?

parameters.speaker: Lars
parameters.text:
He stares at you as if you'd come back from the dead and told him it was a hobby. 'I don't understand what you *do*, son.' Disbelief first, as with Telemachus, who wouldn't believe the beggar at the door was his father. 'A man needs a title. People ask.'

Then, halfway through a sentence about what people ask, he stops. He looks at your hands, and he pulls you into a hug that smells of sap and engine oil. 'I don't understand it,' he says into your shoulder. 'But I can see you love it. I can see that much.'

He hasn't found the name for your craft. He has found you, and that comes first.

parameters.message:
**Telemachus**

Disbelief, then embrace. Your father still doesn't have a word for what you do, but his pride has started to drift from the title toward the person. The team-lead role is held by ${roleHolderName}.

*Questions to carry home:* Does recognition need understanding, or only attention? Can new, AI-mediated work count as real know-how if those closest to you can't see it? Who paid for the choices you made, and did you think to ask them?

beats.name: Argos: Only the Old Work Knows You

parameters.text:
Your father introduces you to the neighbours as 'my son, the one in AI.' He means it kindly. He asks about the title twice. He doesn't ask about the work.

Later your phone buzzes. It's Ines: *'billing went down again, i caught it before the model did. felt the too-clean thing. thought of you.'* And there in the old repository your retry loop still runs, unchanged three years on, doing its quiet job.

Like old Argos on the dung heap, the only ones who recognise you are the work itself and the one person who learned it from you. Your father, out in the orchard, doesn't. Not yet.

parameters.message:
**Argos**

The craft is alive. The work remembers you, and so does Ines. The team-lead role is held by ${roleHolderName}. Your father's pride is real, but it is still fixed on the title.

*Questions to carry home:* Is it enough to be recognised by the work itself? What would a ladder look like that let a parent see a child rise by going deeper? And what would your father need from you, a token like the trees, to see your hands in work that leaves no trace of them?

parameters.text:
You stand in the orchard while your father talks about the title. He talks about what to tell people at the club, about your grandad's forklift, about up. You try once to explain, and the words come out as Graeber words and Naur words, knowing-that words for a knowing-how thing. You watch them slide off him.

So you stop. You say nothing, the way Ajax said nothing in the Underworld. He says nothing back. Two craftsmen who never found the token, standing among trees one of them can name and the other has forgotten.

characters.name: Odie Marsh
characters.description: Twenty-nine. An AI-assisted coder and self-described 'slopling' who loves the work itself: coaxing, steering and catching the model's mistakes. He is offered a team-lead role he isn't sure he wants. Quiet, observant, funny about himself, longing to be seen.

goals.name: Keep the craft alive
goals.description: Keep his know-how and Naur-theory alive by practising it

goals.name: Be seen by his father
goals.description: Have his father's pride attach to who he is, not to his title

goals.name: Climb, as everyone expects
goals.description: The ladder's goal, inherited rather than chosen

characters.name: Lars Marsh
characters.description: Odie's father. A former toolmaker at the Hendry works who became a foreman at thirty-four and never stood at a lathe again. Son of a forklift driver; for his generation, a title meant the family had finally risen above being 'hands'. Now grafts apple trees in an orchard behind the house. Says little; his pride is real but fixed on the visible. Seen mostly through his son's guesses.

goals.name: See his son succeed
goals.description: What success means is the open question

characters.name: Dana Okafor
characters.description: Odie's engineering manager. Warm, harried, genuinely fond of her people, fluent in the ladder's language and half-aware of its absurdity. A warm studio-comedy boss by type only.

goals.name: Fill the team-lead role by end of quarter

characters.name: Chad Bellweather
characters.description: A smooth political colleague: quick, charming, a reader of rooms. The Odysseus of the open-plan office, whose polymetis the ladder rewards. A suitor by type, not a villain.

characters.name: Dougie Pratt
characters.description: A cheerful colleague who has never finished a feature and has never been in the room when one failed. Fails upward by type; farce, not malice.

characters.name: Ines Duarte
characters.description: A junior engineer who sends questions at 11 p.m. and learns best from Odie. Could become his apprentice, the person in whom his theory lives on.

characters.name: Andrei Karpathi
characters.description: A fictionalized, drifted-name version of the AI researcher who coined the term 'vibe coding'. Playful, curious, generous and honest about the limits of his own idea. A guide who both blesses and takes apart Odie's craft.

characters.name: Fred Brookes
characters.description: A fictionalized elder who said yes to managing a vast software project and then wrote down what it cost. Courteous, precise, wry.

characters.name: Linos Torwald
characters.description: A fictionalized version of a famous open-source creator who drifted into management without choosing it, and who publicly committed in 2018 to learning to read people better. The Siren of the Inbox Sea: mild, frank, not unhappy.

characters.name: Ken Tomson
characters.description: A fictionalized legendary systems programmer at Bell Works who saw management as an umbrella, not a seat of power. Dry, amused, absorbed in small perfect things.

characters.name: Claude Shanning
characters.description: A fictionalized playful genius who rides a unicycle, juggles and builds a maze-solving mechanical mouse called Theseus. Joy incarnate, and a lotus risk.

characters.name: Ilya Sutskov
characters.description: A fictionalized researcher-shaman who chants 'Feel the AGI!' and became a CEO anyway. Kind, intense, unsettling, a little tired.

characters.name: Gabe Newall
characters.description: A fictionalized founder of Vane, a company with no managers, around whom everything still orbits. Relaxed, kind, very obviously the sun.

characters.name: Jon Carmick
characters.description: A fictionalized legendary programmer who left the vast court of Metta for small, hands-on Sharp Labs. Blunt, brilliant, free, and sometimes lonely.

characters.name: Denis Hassaby
characters.description: A fictionalized scientist-founder of DeepMound who rewrote his own role from CEO to chairman and chief scientist, part of a lifelong pattern of stepping back toward the work. Warm, honest about the costs. Keeper of Calypso's golden room.

characters.name: Don Knuthe
characters.description: A fictionalized gentle master of computing whose job is to be on the bottom of things rather than on top of them. Cheerful, patient, without an inbox.

characters.name: Ajax
characters.description: The steady craftsman-warrior of Troy, who lost Achilles' armour to the better talker and went mad. In the Underworld he refuses to speak.
